title: Orthogonal Vectors Hypothesis
formal:
Is it true that
\[\forall\varepsilon\in(0,1)\ \exists c\in\mathbb N_{>0}:\ \text{no allowed algorithm solves bichromatic Orthogonal Vectors in }O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\text{ time}\]
for all integers \(n\ge2\) on two lists of \(n\) vectors in \(\{0,1\}^{d}\), where \(d=\lceil c\log_2n\rceil\)? An allowed algorithm is a uniform randomized classical word-RAM program in the model below. Its running-time bound is worst-case over both inputs and random choices, and its answer must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input. The dimension constant \(c\) may depend on the proposed exponent saving \(\varepsilon\), but is fixed as \(n\) grows.
definitions:
Decision problem. For \(n\ge2\), the input consists of ordered lists \(A=(a^{(1)},\ldots,a^{(n)})\) and \(B=(b^{(1)},\ldots,b^{(n)})\) of binary vectors of common dimension \(d=\lceil c\log_2n\rceil\). Repeated vectors, zero vectors and overlap between the lists are allowed. Output YES exactly when
\[\exists r,s\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:\quad\sum_{j=1}^{d}a^{(r)}_j b^{(s)}_j=0.\]
The sum is an ordinary nonnegative integer sum. Equivalently, the two supports are disjoint. Orthogonality modulo two is a different predicate. The selected pair must come from opposite lists, but the task only asks for a decision bit, not for a witness. There is no promise on Hamming weights, intersections, number of solutions or input distribution.

Words and encoding. A machine fixes an integer \(\lambda\ge2\) and uses unsigned words of
\[w=\lambda\lceil\log_2(n+d+2)\rceil\]
bits. Input headers supply \(n,d\), followed by the two lists in order. Each vector occupies \(\lceil d/w\rceil\) consecutive words, with its coordinates packed from least to most significant bit and unused final bits zero. Thus for fixed \(c\) one vector occupies a constant number of words as \(n\) grows. The input is explicit, not supplied by a membership or inner-product oracle. Changing between ordinary explicit bit arrays and this packing costs at most a logarithmic factor; the stated acceptance bound itself uses the packed model.

Instruction set and cost. The program is finite and independent of \(n\). It has word registers and random-access memory addressed by single words. One step may read or write a constant number of addressed words; perform addition, subtraction or multiplication modulo \(2^w\); perform unsigned integer quotient or remainder with a nonzero divisor; apply bitwise AND, OR, XOR or NOT; shift logically left or right; compare words; or branch using a comparison. Shifts discard overflow and give zero when their shift count is at least \(w\). A fresh uniform random \(w\)-bit word costs one step and is independent of all previous random words. A compound operation on several words must be built from these instructions and charged accordingly. There is no unit-cost arbitrary-precision arithmetic, real arithmetic, vector instruction of input-dependent width, or additional oracle.

Uniformity, memory and preprocessing. Outside the explicit input, memory initially contains only zeros. Programs may contain fixed finite constants, but receive no advice, precomputed tables or extra data depending on \(n\). Any such tables must be produced during the charged computation. The program and \(\lambda\) may depend on the fixed \(c\) and \(\varepsilon\), as may constants in the running-time bound; none may vary with \(n\). Single-word addressing bounds available memory by \(2^w\) words. Reading input, constructing tables, preprocessing either list, generating randomness and producing the answer are all charged. There is no separate free preprocessing phase.

Time and error. To solve the problem, the program must halt with a decision bit on every allowed input and random execution. For each fixed input, over its independent internal random words, the bit must equal the predicate above with probability at least \(2/3\). Either type of error is allowed within this bound. The claim \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) means that there exist a real \(K>0\) and an integer \(n_0\ge2\) such that every input of every size \(n\ge n_0\), and every sequence of random choices, takes at most \(K n^{2-\varepsilon}\) steps. An expected-time or average-input bound is not itself this worst-case guarantee. Deterministic programs are included by ignoring the random instruction.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this lower-bound proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must cover every allowed uniform randomized program in the specified instruction model, with the quantifier order \(\forall\varepsilon\,\exists c\) and the per-input success requirement. A proof conditional on an unproved version of the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis is evidence for the conjecture, not an unconditional resolution.

A refutation must establish
\[\exists\varepsilon\in(0,1)\ \forall c\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \exists A_c,\lambda_c,K_c,n_{0,c}:\quad A_c\text{ meets the stated time and correctness conditions}.\]
The same positive saving \(\varepsilon\) must work for every fixed \(c\). The programs, word-size constants, multiplicative constants and asymptotic thresholds may depend on \(c\). Each \(A_c\) must be uniform in \(n\); no additional uniform algorithm taking \(c\) as input is demanded. A deterministic family would also refute the randomized hypothesis.

An exponent saving \(\varepsilon_c>0\) that shrinks with \(c\), a bound for a fixed small dimension, logarithmic improvements over quadratic time, success only on random instances, or a lower bound restricted to monotone circuits, formulas or branching programs does not settle the full proposition. A fast online query bound with separate preprocessing must satisfy the total charged offline time before it qualifies. This is an asymptotic yes-or-no claim, with no additive numerical approximation tolerance.
why: A basic disjointness problem anchors a large part of fine-grained complexity. Settling its uniform exponent barrier would reshape conditional lower bounds for strings, geometry and data structures.

importance.reason: One of the principal hypotheses organizing polynomial-time lower bounds across multiple algorithmic areas, with an elementary explicit task and precise dimension dependence.

progress.text: Abboud–Williams–Yu obtain dimension-dependent truly subquadratic algorithms via the polynomial method; the exponent saving decreases with the dimension constant.
Chan–Williams derandomize the dimension-dependent \(n^{2-1/O(\log c)}\) bound and also count orthogonal pairs. This still does not provide one exponent saving for every \(c\).
Rohatgi develops OV-based conditional hardness for exact Earth Mover Distance, illustrating geometric consequences.
Alman–Andoni–Zhang improve average-case OV algorithms; the work appears at SOSA 2025.
Gajulapalli and coauthors give deterministic online data structures and refute a separate online space/query conjecture; the exponent saving remains dependent on the dimension constant.
Dürr–Kipouridis–Lampis–Węgrzycki publish a one-sided randomized \(\widetilde O(1.25^d n)\) low-dimensional algorithm, with a reported computer-aided \(O(1.16^d n)\) refinement.
Choudhury and coauthors establish the logarithmic-dimension monotone-circuit version for the negated predicate and strengthen other restricted-model lower bounds.

status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. July 2026 Conjecture 1 explicitly retains the unrestricted randomized OV hypothesis while proving circuit, formula and branching-program restrictions. Deterministic and randomized dimension-dependent algorithms remain compatible with its quantifier order. The May online-OV refutation addresses a different space/query conjecture, and average-case algorithms do not cover every input. No matching unrestricted resolution was found in the bounded primary-source search; external proofs were not independently formalized.

context_blocks.text: Each vector can be viewed as a subset of a universe of d coordinates. The task is to find a disjoint pair across two collections. Although checking one pair is easy, there are \(n^{2}\) possible pairs. For logarithmic dimension, packed coordinates make a single check take only a constant number of machine operations when c is fixed. The hypothesis asks whether there is an unavoidable exponent arbitrarily close to two as that fixed dimension constant grows.

The dependence on \(c\) is the main subtlety. Abboud, Williams and Yu’s SODA 2015 algorithm runs in \(n^{2-1/O(\log c)}\) time in the relevant large-\(c\) regime. Thus a positive exponent saving is already known for every fixed dimension constant, but the saving decreases as that constant increases. This is compatible with the hypothesis, which excludes one positive saving shared by all constants. The conference year is 2015, even though some later bibliographies label the paper 2014.

Randomness is not necessary for the existing dimension-dependent saving. Chan and Williams’s SODA 2016 result obtains deterministic \(n^{2-1/O(\log c)}\) time, including counting orthogonal pairs and batched bichromatic detection. It still allows the saving to decrease with \(c\). The hypothesis therefore does not assert that randomization is the only obstacle to a universal subquadratic algorithm.

The ICALP 2026 algorithm has a one-sided-error running-time bound \(\widetilde O(1.25^d n)\), with a reported computer-aided improvement to \(O(1.16^d n)\). Here the tilde suppresses logarithmic factors in the input size, including polynomial factors in \(d\) in the stated logarithmic regime. The finite parameter evaluation was not independently rerun in this review. Exponential dependence on dimension becomes a power of \(n\) after substituting \(d=\lceil c\log_2n\rceil\), so this bound does not give the uniform exponent saving excluded by the hypothesis.

For example, substituting \(c=2\) into \(1.25^{d} n\) gives, up to constant and logarithmic factors, \(n^{1+2 \log _{2} 1.25}\), whose exponent is about 1.644. Increasing c increases this exponent. Thus an impressive subquadratic algorithm for one small logarithmic dimension does not supply one exponent saving for all logarithmic dimensions. This numerical example illustrates the quantifiers; it is not an additional algorithmic theorem.

The corresponding randomized Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis implies this randomized OV hypothesis through the standard satisfiability reduction and sparsification. That supplies a conditional explanation for the proposed barrier, not an unconditional lower bound. A deterministic-only satisfiability assumption cannot by itself rule out randomized OV algorithms. The current primary literature continues to separate these assumptions from the restricted-model theorems it proves.

Reductions then transfer the conjectured time barrier to problems that look quite different. Rohatgi’s Earth Mover Distance paper, the inherited source for this record, develops one such geometric application. The significance of OV is its role as a common intermediate problem: a new algorithm can overturn a collection of conditional barriers, while an unconditional proof would establish a strong lower bound for a concrete problem already known to be in polynomial time.

Restricted-model lower bounds provide evidence without establishing that unrestricted conclusion. Choudhury and coauthors prove near-quadratic monotone-circuit lower bounds for the negation of OV at logarithmic dimension. This negated predicate says every cross-pair intersects and is monotone in the input bits. Their July 2026 paper also strengthens formula and branching-program bounds. General RAM programs can use operations and intermediate representations beyond those restrictions, so these theorems do not prove the hypothesis as formulated here.

Distributional improvements are a separate frontier. Alman, Andoni and Zhang obtain faster algorithms when vector coordinates are independently sampled with a specified Bernoulli bias, including difficult parameter ranges. Such a result can explain why random instances are easier while leaving adversarial instances unresolved. The card deliberately requires correctness and the stated running time on every input rather than only on a random input distribution.

The May 2026 online-OV paper deterministically refutes a different conjecture about preprocessing space and later query time. Its logarithmic-dimensional query saving depends on \(c\), and preprocessing has its own stated cost. The offline decision problem here is charged for both lists and every preprocessing step. The word “refutation” in that paper consequently does not mean the present OV hypothesis was refuted.

sentences: Bichromatic Orthogonal Vectors asks whether two explicit lists contain binary vectors with disjoint supports.
The retained hypothesis says that every proposed fixed saving over quadratic time fails at some fixed logarithmic-dimension constant.
It concerns uniform randomized word-RAM algorithms with all preprocessing charged, worst-case running time and bounded error on every input.
A complete Lean refutation must provide one positive exponent saving valid for every dimension constant, although its individual programs and time constants may depend on that constant.
Known deterministic and randomized dimension-dependent savings, average-case improvements and restricted-model lower bounds leave this full hypothesis unresolved.

source_formulation.text: Rohatgi’s inherited source states a randomized OV conjecture for a superlogarithmic dimension function. The existing card selected the standard logarithmic-dimension formulation with the order “for every exponent saving, some fixed dimension constant”; July 2026 Conjecture 1 states exactly that order and explicitly includes randomized algorithms. This review retains that selected variant, bichromatic lists, packed inputs, worst-case running time, category and importance 96. It makes the word-RAM operations and parameter dependencies explicit, without claiming that the different dimension formulations are identical solely by renaming parameters.
